messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meena is a 44-year-old retail worker who lives with her husband in a quiet suburban neighborhood. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during a routine evening shift at the department store where she stocks shelves. She was walking through the home-goods aisle when she heard a commotion near the register—raised voices, then a single sharp crack that she later learned was a gunshot. A customer had collapsed, shot during an attempted robbery. Meena did not see the shooter, but she saw the aftermath: the man on the floor, the spreading dark stain, the paramedics working frantically. She was not injured, but she stood frozen for what felt like an eternity, unable to move or look away.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that moment refused to settle into a clear sequence. When Meena tries to piece together what happened, the images come in fragments—the tile floor, the paramedic's voice, the color of the man's shirt—but she cannot arrange them in order. What stays with her most powerfully is not the factual sequence but the overwhelming grief that floods her when she remembers. She finds herself weeping without warning, the emotion as fresh as if the event were still happening. When the memory returns, it is so overwhelming that she has to stop whatever she is doing, unable to speak or move until the wave passes.

Meena has come to believe that her mind is broken, that she cannot trust her own memory or her own reactions. This fear has driven her to scan her surroundings constantly, watching for any sign of threat. At work, she finds herself checking the exits, studying customers' faces, listening for raised voices. The hypervigilance is exhausting, but she is certain that if she lets her guard down, something terrible will happen again. She has become easily startled—a dropped box in the stockroom makes her heart race for minutes afterward. The more she scans for danger, the more the memory of that night intrudes, as if her vigilance itself triggers the images and the grief.

The memory loops back into her strategies in a tightening spiral. When the overwhelming recall hits—usually after a customer raises their voice or after she hears a sound that reminds her of that night—Meena finds herself thinking obsessively about why this happened to her, searching for a meaning that never arrives. She has also begun to go along with whatever others want, agreeing to extra shifts, staying late, never saying no. She has come to believe that if she keeps everyone around her happy, she will be safe. But this people-pleasing only heightens her sense of being out of control, which makes her scan even more vigilantly, which in turn makes the memories more vivid and frequent.

The cycle has worn her down. She rarely talks about the event with anyone, but when she does—when a coworker asks what happened that night—the act of speaking about it triggers the memory so powerfully that she becomes dizzy, lightheaded, her vision swimming. She has started crying at unpredictable moments, sometimes in the break room, sometimes at home while watching television, and she cannot explain why. The dizziness and the crying have become additional triggers, so that now even her own emotional and physical responses can send her back into the fragmented, grief-soaked memory.

Meena's husband has noticed the change. She used to be warm and talkative; now she is watchful and withdrawn. She has stopped visiting her sister, who lives in the city, because the drive feels too exposed. At work, she has been written up twice for leaving her station without explanation—she had been overwhelmed by a sudden memory and needed to hide in the bathroom until it passed. She is terrified that she will lose her job, but she is more terrified that something will happen again and she will freeze, unable to protect herself or anyone else. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when her husband found her sobbing in the laundry room, unable to say why. She looked at him and said, "I think I'm losing my mind." She is afraid that is true. But somewhere underneath that fear is a quieter hope: that someone can help her make sense of the fragments, and that the grief might one day stop arriving without warning.
